blocks.content: # Robust Adaptive Backup Control Barrier Functions
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Ersin Da $\mathrm{s}^{1}$ , David E. J. van Wijk $^{2}$ , Tamas G. Molnar $^{3}$ , Aaron D. Ames $^{2}$ , and Joel W. Burdick $^{2}$
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Abstract—We propose a notion of robust adaptive backup control barrier functions for nonlinear control affine systems with parametric uncertainty in both the drift dynamics and actuation matrix. Backup control barrier functions guarantee safety by predicting the system's trajectory under a pre-certified safe controller. However, these predictions rely on the model and can be inaccurate when the system contains unknown parameters. To address this issue, we estimate the unknown parameters using element-wise certified adaptive estimators that provide a parameter adaptation law and component-wise estimation error bounds. We compute the backup flow using the estimated model and tighten the safety conditions using these certified bounds. The resulting safety conditions account for the sensitivity of the predicted flow to parameter estimation errors. Moreover, to handle uncertainty in the actuation matrix, we use a duality-based reformulation that enables the use of a computationally efficient quadratic-program-based safety filter. We prove that controllers satisfying the proposed robust adaptive backup control barrier function constraints guarantee safety under parametric uncertainty and input constraints.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: ## I. INTRODUCTION
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Safety-critical control is essential for autonomous systems that operate in complex real-world environments. Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a constructive framework for synthesizing controllers that render a prescribed safe set forward invariant, ensuring safety w.r.t. state constraints [1]. This can be realized by safety filters, often formulated as quadratic programs (QPs), that modify a nominal controller when safety necessitates intervention. However, CBF design requires a safe set in which feasible safe control inputs are available. Constructing such a set is difficult for input-constrained nonlinear systems, especially when the system must be steered close to the safe set boundary [2], [3].
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Model predictive control (MPC) provides another way to handle state and input constraints. It predicts the system evolution over a finite horizon while enforcing constraints along the predicted trajectory. This makes MPC effective for constrained nonlinear systems, but recursive feasibility and safety guarantees require additional terminal conditions, invariant sets, or robustness margins. Adaptive MPC and robust sensitivity-based MPC reduce conservatism by updating model information online [4] -[6] or by propagating the effect of parametric uncertainty along the prediction horizon [7].
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Backup control barrier functions (bCBFs) use a similar finite horizon prediction idea for safety-critical control to construct an implicit safe set online [8]. Instead of requiring an explicit controlled invariant set, bCBFs predict the evolution of the system under a pre-certified safe controller, called a backup controller, over a finite time horizon. A system is considered safe if the predicted backup trajectory satisfies the state constraints and reaches a known backup set [8]. This approach guarantees feasibility for input-constrained systems
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: by providing a constructive certificate that the state remains safe. However, bCBFs rely on forward integration to compute the flow of the system model. Thus, model uncertainty can cause the computed backup trajectory to differ from the true trajectory, invalidating safety [9].
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: This limitation becomes more severe when the uncertainty appears in both the drift dynamics and the actuation matrix. Actuation uncertainty complicates robust safety filter design because the worst-case uncertainty involves the control input that is the decision variable of the underlying optimization problem. Recent robust CBF methods address related issues by using worst-case bounds, set-membership identification, or duality-based reformulations [10], [11]. Adaptive CBF methods reduce conservatism by estimating uncertain parameters online [12], [13]. However, robust bCBFs require more than a pointwise estimate of uncertain parameters. Since the safety condition depends on the predicted backup flow, it must account for the sensitivity of the flow to the parameter estimation errors. Moreover, if the estimator returns only a set-valued update, it may not provide the parameter estimate required for computing the backup flow sensitivity.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: In this letter, we propose a robust adaptive bCBF framework for nonlinear systems with structured parametric uncertainty in the drift dynamics and actuation matrix. We consider a parameter affine uncertainty model and use element-wise certified adaptive estimators. These estimators provide a parameter adaptation law and certified component-wise bounds on the parameter estimation error. The proposed method computes the backup flow using the estimated model and tightens the safety conditions using the certified error bounds. These tightened conditions define an inner approximation of the implicit safe set. To handle uncertainty in the actuation matrix, we use a duality-based robustification that preserves a QP-based safety filter. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through a planar quadrotor example.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: ## II. PRELIMINARIES
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: We consider a nonlinear control affine system of the form
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\dot {\boldsymbol {x}} = \boldsymbol {f} (\boldsymbol {x}) + \boldsymbol {g} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u}, \quad \boldsymbol {x} \in \mathcal {X} \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {n}, \quad \boldsymbol {u} \in \mathcal {U} \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: where $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\boldsymbol{g}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ are continuously differentiable, and $\mathcal{U}$ is a convex polytope. To capture state constraints that characterize safety, we define the safe set
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\mathcal {C} _ {\mathrm {S}} \triangleq \left\{\boldsymbol {x} \in \mathcal {X}: h (\boldsymbol {x}) \geq 0 \right\},
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: where $h : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuously differentiable. Safety requires that (1) evolves inside the safe set, i.e., $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ must be forward invariant. Control barrier functions (CBFs) enable the synthesis of safe controllers. The function $h$ is a CBF if there exists an extended class-$\mathcal{K}_{\infty}$ function $\alpha$ such that
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\sup _ {\boldsymbol {u} \in \mathcal {U}} \left[ \nabla h (\boldsymbol {x}) \left(\boldsymbol {f} (\boldsymbol {x}) + \boldsymbol {g} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u}\right) \right] > - \alpha \left(h (\boldsymbol {x})\right),
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: holds for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ . Then, any locally Lipschitz controller $\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{k}(\boldsymbol{x})$ , $\boldsymbol{k}: \mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{U}$ , satisfying
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\nabla h (\boldsymbol {x}) \left(\boldsymbol {f} (\boldsymbol {x}) + \boldsymbol {g} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u}\right) \geq - \alpha \left(h (\boldsymbol {x})\right), \quad \forall \boldsymbol {x} \in \mathcal {C} _ {\mathrm {S}},
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: renders $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ forward invariant [1], ensuring the safety of (1).
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: While CBFs provide a systematic way to synthesize safe controllers, an arbitrary safety function $h$ may not satisfy the CBF condition (3), especially with bounded inputs. In this case, there may exist states in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ for which there is no admissible input satisfying the constraint (4). Backup CBFs [8] address this issue by constructing a subset of $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ where safe inputs are guaranteed to exist and by generating corresponding safe controllers within the CBF framework.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: The backup CBF method leverages a backup controller and a backup set that typically represent safe but conservative behavior. Let $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{B}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ be a backup set, defined by
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\mathcal {C} _ {\mathrm {B}} \triangleq \left\{\boldsymbol {x} \in \mathcal {X}: h _ {\mathrm {b}} (\boldsymbol {x}) \geq 0 \right\},
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: with a continuously differentiable safety function $h_{\mathrm{b}}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $k_{\mathrm{b}}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{U}$ be a backup controller that renders $C_{\mathrm{B}}$ forward invariant. The closed-loop dynamics under $k_{\mathrm{b}}$ are $\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)k_{\mathrm{b}}(x)$, and the backup flow $\varphi_{\mathrm{b}}(\tau ,x)$ denotes the solution of this system starting from state $x$, over time $\tau \in [0,T]$ with a backup horizon $T > 0$.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: The key idea of bCBFs is to define the implicit safe set
blocks.label: Text
Formula

blocks.content: This represents the states from which the system can safely reach the backup set in time $T$ via the backup controller. The set $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}$ is a subset of $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ , and it is forward invariant under the backup controller. Therefore, by construction, safe inputs are guaranteed to exist in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}$ . This construction is useful for input-constrained systems because feasibility can be inherited from the backup controller [8].
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: ## III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: We extend bCBFs to systems with model uncertainty as
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\dot {\boldsymbol {x}} = \boldsymbol {f} (\boldsymbol {x}) + \boldsymbol {g} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u} + \Delta \boldsymbol {f} (\boldsymbol {x}) + \Delta \boldsymbol {g} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u},
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: where $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\boldsymbol{g}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ are the known nominal components of the dynamics, while $\Delta f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\Delta g:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ represent unknown structured uncertainty in the drift vector field and actuation matrix. We assume that the uncertainty admits the parameter affine representation
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\Delta \boldsymbol {f} (\boldsymbol {x}) = \boldsymbol {F} (\boldsymbol {x}) \theta_ {\mathrm {f}}, \quad \Delta \boldsymbol {g} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N _ {\mathrm {g}}} \boldsymbol {G} _ {j} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u} \theta_ {\mathrm {g}, j},
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: where $\boldsymbol{F}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times N_{\mathrm{f}}}$ and $G_{j}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ are known terms, while $\theta_{\mathrm{f}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathrm{f}}}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\hat{N}_{\mathrm{g}}}$ are unknown parameters.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Collecting the parameters in a vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ such that $\boldsymbol{\theta}\triangleq\left[ \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{f}}^{\top}\quad\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{g}}^{\top}\right]^{\top}=[\theta_{1}\quad\theta_{2}\quad\dots\quad\theta_{N}]^{\top},$ with $N=N_{\mathrm{f}}+N_{\mathrm{g}}$ parameters, and by defining a regression matrix as
blocks.label: Text
Formula

blocks.content:
$$
\phi (\boldsymbol {x}, \boldsymbol {u}) \triangleq [ \boldsymbol {F} (\boldsymbol {x}) \quad \boldsymbol {G} _ {1} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u} \quad \dots \quad \boldsymbol {G} _ {N _ {\mathrm {g}}} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u} ],
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: system (7) can be written compactly as
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\dot {\boldsymbol {x}} = \boldsymbol {f} (\boldsymbol {x}) + \boldsymbol {g} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {u} + \phi (\boldsymbol {x}, \boldsymbol {u}) \theta .
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: The uncertainty representation in (10) is essential for our subsequent results. In particular, the control direction uncertainty term $\Delta g ( x ) u$ will preserve affine dependence on the control input in the robust bCBF conditions and is therefore critical for constructing a QP-based safety filter.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: While $\theta$ is unknown, it represents fixed coefficients that parameterize model uncertainty, a structure also common to
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: adaptive and learning-based control. In robotic systems, these coefficients often correspond to physical quantities or model mismatches, such as damping coefficients, gravity mismatch mass or inertia errors, for which conservative ranges can be obtained from system identification, nominal specifications, or physical limits. Accordingly, we assume that we know lower and upper bounds on each component of $\theta$ .
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Assumption 1. There exist known constants $\theta_{i}^{-},\theta_{i}^{+}\in\mathbb{R}$ for $i\in\{1,\dots,N\}$ such that $\theta_{i}^{-}\leq \theta_{i}\leq \theta_{i}^{+}.$ Therefore, $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\Theta,$ where $\Theta\triangleq[\theta_{1}^{-},\theta_{1}^{+}] \times\cdots\times[\theta_{N}^{-},\theta_{N}^{+}].$
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Given Assumption 1, the unknown parameter $\theta$ will be estimated, and the estimate will be used for safe control design. The proposed safety result does not require a specific adaptive law for estimation. Instead, it requires a differentiable parameter estimate and certified component-wise bounds on the estimation error. We next define an estimator class that can provide the required estimate and bounds.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Let $\mathcal{H}_{t}$ denote the measured state and input data history available at time t, which may contain filtered regressions integral regressions, or stored data. These data are used for calculating an estimate $\hat{\theta}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ of the parameter $\theta$ . We consider general parameter estimation dynamics of the form
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\dot {\hat {\theta}} = q \left(\hat {\theta}, \mathcal {H} _ {t}, t\right).
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: Assume the estimator is initialized as $\hat{\theta} (0)\in\Theta$ and satisfies
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\hat {\theta} (t) \in \Theta , \quad \forall t \geq 0.
$$
blocks.label: Formula

An estimator satisfying (11) and (12) is an element-wise certified adaptive estimator if it provides a known signal $\boldsymbol{\rho}(t)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}^{N}$ such that the estimation error $\tilde{\theta}(t)\triangleq\boldsymbol{\theta}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(t)$ satisfies

$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: with $\boldsymbol{A}\triangleq[\boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{I}]^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}(t)\triangleq\left[ \boldsymbol{\rho}(t)^{\top}\quad\boldsymbol{\rho}(t)^{\top}\right]^{\top}.$ Note that, since $\theta,\hat{\theta}(t)\in\Theta$ , the bounds satisfy $\rho_{i}(t)\leq\theta_{i}^{+}-\theta_{i}^{-}.$
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Example 1 (Dynamic regressor extension and mixing (DREM) parameter estimator [14], [15]). Consider a linear regression $y_{\mathrm{r}}(t)=m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\top}(t)\theta$ where $y_{\mathrm{r}}(t)\in \mathbb{R}$ and $m_{\mathrm{r}}(t)\in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ are known. DREM estimator estimates a parameter in two steps. First, the extension step constructs known signals $Y_{\mathrm{e}}(t)\in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ and $M_{\mathrm{e}}(t)\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ satisfying $Y_{\mathrm{e}}(t)=M_{\mathrm{e}}(t)\theta$ . This extended regression can be obtained, for example, by stacking the original regression with filtered regressions generated by stable linear operators [14]. Second, the mixing step multiplies the extended regression by the adjugate of $M_{\mathrm{e}}(t)$ as $Y_{\mathrm{D}}(t)\triangleq\operatorname{adj}(M_{\mathrm{e}}(t))Y_{\mathrm{e}}(t).$ By defining $\chi(t)\triangleq\det(M_{\mathrm{e}}(t))$ , it can be shown that $Y_{\mathrm{D}}(t)=\chi(t)\theta$ holds because $\operatorname{adj}(M_{\mathrm{e}})M_{\mathrm{e}}=\det(M_{\mathrm{e}})I_{N}.$ Then, each parameter is estimated with the update law
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\dot {\hat {\theta}} _ {i} (t) = \gamma_ {i} \chi (t) \left(Y _ {\mathrm {D}, i} (t) - \chi (t) \hat {\theta} _ {i} (t)\right), \quad \gamma_ {i} > 0,
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\dot {\tilde {\theta}} _ {i} (t) = - \gamma_ {i} \chi^ {2} (t) \tilde {\theta} _ {i} (t).
$$

For instance, recursive least-squares estimators with zonotopic uncertainty propagation also provide an adaptation law with a set-valued uncertainty certificate [13]. More generally, any adaptive, composite learning, or set-membership estimator can be used if it provides the adaptation law in (11) and an element-wise bound [11], [13].

blocks.content: We are now in a position to state the considered problem, which will be addressed using robust adaptive bCBFs.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Problem 1. Given the uncertain system (10), the safe set $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ in (2), and an element-wise certified adaptive estimator (11), design a control law $\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{k}(t,\boldsymbol{x},\hat{\theta})\in\mathcal{U}$ that renders a subset of $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ forward invariant, ensuring the safety of (10).
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: ## IV. MAIN RESULTS
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: We now develop the proposed robust adaptive bCBF method in four steps. First, we propagate the backup flow using the current parameter estimate. Second, we bound the mismatch between the true and estimated backup flows using the certified component-wise parameter error bounds. Third, we use this bound to define a tightened inner approximation of the implicit safe set. Fourth, we derive duality-based robust safety conditions that preserve a QP implementation.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Similar to the standard bCBF method outlined in Section II, the proposed approach leverages a backup controller $k_{\mathrm{b}} : \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{U}$ and a backup set $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{B}}\subseteq \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ given in (5). This time, we assume that $k_{\mathrm{b}}$ is a robust backup controller.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Assumption 2. The backup controller $k_{\mathrm{b}}$ renders $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{B}}$ forward invariant for (10) for any $\theta\in\Theta.$
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: In practice, robust backup sets can often be obtained by robustifying Lyapunov level sets around a stabilizable equilibrium point and verifying their invariance under the corresponding stabilizing feedback control law [9]. In Section V, we utilize this approach to synthesize a robust backup controller and a robust backup set for a quadrotor model.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: We introduce the closed-loop dynamics of the system (10) under the robust backup controller as
blocks.label: Text

$$
\dot {\boldsymbol {x}} = \boldsymbol {f} _ {\mathrm {b}} (\boldsymbol {x}, \theta) \triangleq \boldsymbol {f} (\boldsymbol {x}) + \boldsymbol {g} (\boldsymbol {x}) \boldsymbol {k} _ {\mathrm {b}} (\boldsymbol {x}) + \psi_ {\mathrm {b}} (\boldsymbol {x}) \theta ,
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: where $\psi_{\mathrm{b}}$ indicates the regression matrix in (9) evaluated along the backup controller:
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\psi_ {\mathrm {b}} (\boldsymbol {x}) \triangleq \phi (\boldsymbol {x}, k _ {\mathrm {b}} (\boldsymbol {x})).
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: Then, the backup flow satisfies
blocks.label: Text

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial \tau} \varphi_ {\mathrm {b}} (\tau , \boldsymbol {x}) = f _ {\mathrm {b}} \left(\varphi_ {\mathrm {b}} (\tau , \boldsymbol {x}), \theta\right), \quad \varphi_ {\mathrm {b}} (0, \boldsymbol {x}) = \boldsymbol {x}.
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: Ideally, one would use the backup flow to enforce the forward invariance of the implicit safe set $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}$ defined in (6). However, since the parameter $\theta$ is unknown, the backup flow $\varphi_{\mathrm{b}}$ and the implicit set $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}$ may not be known. Therefore, we instead establish a known subset of $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}$ and enforce the forward invariance thereof. To this end, we propagate an estimated backup flow $\widehat{\varphi}_{\mathrm{b}}$ using the current parameter estimate $\hat{\theta}(t)$ that is frozen over the backup horizon:
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial \tau} \widehat {\varphi} _ {\mathrm {b}} (\tau , \boldsymbol {x}, t) = \boldsymbol {f} _ {\mathrm {b}} \left(\widehat {\varphi} _ {\mathrm {b}} (\tau , \boldsymbol {x}, t), \hat {\theta} (t)\right), \quad \widehat {\varphi} _ {\mathrm {b}} (0, \boldsymbol {x}, t) = \boldsymbol {x}.
$$
blocks.label: Formula

blocks.content: While the estimated flow $\hat{\varphi}_{\mathrm{b}}$ is known, it is not sufficient for ensuring safety by itself, since the true parameter $\theta$ can differ from the estimated parameter $\hat{\theta}$ . Therefore, we bound the difference between the true and estimated backup flows:
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content:
$$
\left\| \varphi_ {\mathrm {b}} (\tau , \boldsymbol {x}) - \widehat {\varphi} _ {\mathrm {b}} (\tau , \boldsymbol {x}, t) \right\| \leq \delta_ {\varphi} (\tau , \boldsymbol {x}, t),
$$

Consider the uncertain system (10), an estimator in Definition 1, the safe set $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ in (2), the backup controller $k_{\mathrm{b}}$ , the backup set $C_{\mathrm{B}}$ in (5), and the time-varying set $\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ in (25). Suppose Assumptions 1 and 2 hold Then, any locally Lipschitz controller satisfying (31)-(34) for all $\tau\in[0,T]$ renders $\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ forward invariant for (10). Consequently, every closed-loop trajectory starting in $\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{I}}(0)$ remains in $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ : $\mathbf{x}(0)\in\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{I}}(0)\Rightarrow\mathbf{x}(t)\in C_{\mathrm{S}}$ $\forall t\geq0.$

blocks.content: Proof. By strong duality, the dual inequality and equality conditions in (31)-(34) imply the primal robust inequalities (29) and (30). Since $\tilde{\theta} ( t ) \in\widetilde{\Theta} ( t )$ , these primal inequalities imply (27). Consequently, the comparison lemma gives the forward invariance of $\widehat{C_{\mathrm{I}}}(t)$ . From the tightening construction (23), we have $\widehat{C_{\mathrm{I}}}(t) \subseteq C_{\mathrm{I}}$ . Since $\tau=0$ is included in the definition of $C_{\mathrm{I}}$ , we also have $C_{\mathrm{I}}\subseteq C_{\mathrm{S}}$ . Therefore, every closed-loop trajectory starting in $\widehat{C_{\mathrm{I}}}(0)$ remains in $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ .

Let the backup horizon be discretized by $\tau_{j} = jT / N_{T}$ for $j\in \{0,\dots,N_T\}$, and define the decision variable vector as $w\triangleq \left(u,\{\mu_{\tau_j}\}_{j=0}^{N_T},\mu_{\mathrm{b}}\right)$ that contains $N_w\triangleq m + (N_T + 2)2N$ elements. With $w$, we formulate an adaptive safety filter that minimally modifies a potentially unsafe primary controller $k_{\mathrm{p}}:\mathcal{X}\to \mathcal{U}$ into a safe controller:

Formula

blocks.content: Note that (35) is a QP, since its constraints are affine in w. Remark 1. Theorem 1 uses continuous time safety conditions over $\tau\in[0,T]$ , while the QP in (35) enforces discretized constraints on a grid using $\tau_{j}$ . As in standard bCBF implementations, one can add inter-sample margins or choose a sufficiently fine grid to account for the discretization error.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Remark 2. The proposed method with the QP in (35) ensures safety without requiring the notoriously restrictive persistent excitation (PE) condition on the regression matrix. Furthermore, as the certified bounds $\rho_{i}(t)$ decrease, the flow error bound $\delta_{\varphi}$ and the tightening terms $\epsilon,\epsilon_{\mathrm{b}}$ shrink; therefore, the inner approximation $\widehat{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}}(t)$ approaches $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}$ as $\rho_{i}(t)\rightarrow 0.$
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Remark 3. Since the set $\widehat{C}_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ is not necessarily controlled invariant by construction, the QP in (35) can be infeasible for
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: some $t \geq 0$ because of the input bounds or the emptiness of the set $\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ . Note that the non-emptiness of $\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ depends on the size of the tightening terms $\epsilon, \epsilon_{\mathrm{b}}$ , which are largest at $t=0$ and shrink as the certified bounds $\rho_{i}(t)$ decrease. In practice, $\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ can be made non-empty by choosing a sufficiently short backup horizon $T$ or a sufficiently tight initial parameter box $\Theta$ , and becomes progressively less conservative as the estimator refines the parameter estimate. To ensure robust safety in the case of potential infeasibility of the QP, the robust backup controller $k_{\mathrm{b}}$ can be utilized. By Assumption 2, $k_{\mathrm{b}}$ renders $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}$ forward invariant along (10), and satisfies $k_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathcal{U}$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}$ . Therefore, if (35) becomes infeasible, one can switch to $k_{\mathrm{b}}$ to keep the state in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ while satisfying the input constraints. A smooth switching between $k^{\star}$ and $k_{\mathrm{b}}$ can also be used, as in [19].

blocks.content: Fig. 1 shows a simulation of the planar quadrotor using the proposed robust adaptive bCBF and the DREM estimator of Example 1. We compare our method against two baselines: the primary controller $k_{\mathrm{p}}$ alone, and the nominal bCBF method of Section II that propagates the backup flow with the nominal model $(\theta =0)$ and applies no tightening or robustification. The true parameters $\theta= [ 0.08\ 0.08\ 0.22\ -0.32\ 0.008\ 0.003]^{\top}$ correspond to a quadrotor that is approximately 47% heavier than the nominal model; the remaining simulation parameters are provided in the code repository $^{\dagger}$ . As shown in Fig. 1, the primary controller alone enters the unsafe set. The nominal bCBF intervenes late and violates the surface clearance as the true quadrotor is heavier than the nominal model. On the other hand, the proposed robust adaptive bCBF ensures safety by keeping the quadrotor within $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ and satisfying the input constraints despite parametric uncertainty. This is achieved using the parameter estimates, whose certified bounds shrink over time. Accordingly, the estimated backup flows $\widehat{\varphi}_{\mathrm{b}}(\tau ,\boldsymbol{x},t)$ initially deviate from the true backup flows $\varphi_{\mathrm{b}}(\tau ,\boldsymbol{x})$ and later coincide with them as the estimates converge, making the tightening terms vanish and the inner approximation $\widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathrm{I}}(t)$ approach the implicit safe set $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{I}}.$

blocks.content: ## VI. CONCLUSION
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: We presented a robust adaptive backup CBF framework for the safety-critical control of nonlinear systems with parametric uncertainty and bounded inputs. This method computes the backup flow using an online parameter estimate and tightens the backup safety constraints with certified componentwise error bounds. A duality-based robustification yielded a safety filter in the form of a convex QP. Future work will focus on tighter bounds for flow prediction errors.
blocks.label: Text

blocks.content: Finally, we show that $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{B}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}$ . Since $h_{x,\mathrm{b}}(\boldsymbol{x})\geq 0$ and $h_{z,\mathrm{b}}(\boldsymbol{x})\geq 0$ , we have $h_{x}(\boldsymbol{x})\geq r_{x}$ and $h_{z}(\boldsymbol{x})\geq r_{z}.$ Moreover, by the fifth condition in (40), $h_{\vartheta,\mathrm{b}}(\boldsymbol{x})\geq 0$ implies $h_{\vartheta}(\boldsymbol{x})=\vartheta_{\max}^{2}-\vartheta^{2}\geq r_{\vartheta}.$ Therefore, by the last condition in (40), the smooth minimum safety function (37) satisfies $h(\boldsymbol{x})\geq 0$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{B}}$ , i.e., $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{B}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{S}}.$
